analysis.one_liner: Caps the total cost of consumer credit, including fees, at 36% a year.
analysis.headline: The bill had 4 Senate sponsors and no Republican support, and it never received a hearing or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a national 36% annual cap on the cost of consumer credit into federal law, and it counts every fee — late fees, overdraft fees, cash advance fees, credit insurance — toward that cap. Because payday loans average around 400% a year and bank overdraft loans can run far higher, the cap would effectively shut down most high-cost short-term lending. Lenders who broke the cap could face prison time, and borrowers could void the debt entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income borrowers who use payday, car title, overdraft, and high-cost installment loans. The bill's own findings put what these borrowers pay at roughly $14 billion a year on overdraft loans, $9 billion on payday loans, and $3.8 billion on car title loans. Anyone who takes a loan above 36% would have the charges voided and returned. The bill notes Congress already set this same 36% cap for servicemembers in 2006.

how_it_helps.text: No creditor may extend consumer credit where the combined fees and interest exceed 36% a year, and the count includes late fees, overdraft fees, cash advance fees, membership fees, credit insurance, and add-on products — closing the loopholes the bill says let high-cost lending persist in all 50 states.

Any payment on a loan made in violation of the cap is null and void: the creditor must return principal, interest, and fees, and the borrower can raise the violation as a defense to collection or repossession at any time, with no statute of limitations.

Violations carry criminal penalties of up to one year in prison and a fine of the greater of $50,000 or three times the accrued debt, and state attorneys general can sue to enforce the cap in federal court.
States remain free to adopt stricter caps, and credit card statements would replace the APR figure with an all-in rate labeled 'FAIR' so borrowers see the true yearly cost.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, car title, and online installment lenders, and banks that earn overdraft fees, would lose most of their fee and interest revenue on high-cost loans. Some borrowers with poor credit could lose access to small-dollar emergency credit entirely, because lenders may judge that a 36% loan cannot be profitable for them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday, title, installment lenders and overdraft-charging banks

drawbacks.text: A 36% all-in cap, especially one that counts late and overdraft fees, would make most small-dollar lending unprofitable, so borrowers with poor credit who currently use these loans could be left with no legal emergency credit option at all — the bill acknowledges this concern by directing that alternatives encouraging small-dollar loans with minimal fees and affordable repayment schedules be encouraged, but it does not create any.

The bill creates no federal substitute for the credit it bans, so any demand that survives the cap would shift to informal sources such as family loans or unregulated lenders, an outcome critics of rate caps have warned about in comparable state laws.

Overdraft programs, whatever their cost to consumers, function as a source of short-term liquidity at many banks; capping the associated fees removes that cushion for account holders who occasionally overdraw.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large for the millions of borrowers currently paying triple-digit rates: the charges become void and uncollectible, and enforcement is unusually strong for a consumer bill, including criminal penalties and attorney general suits. The honest cost is that a hard cap eliminates a product rather than fixing it — the subprime borrowers most reliant on payday and title loans may lose access to legal credit without a replacement being created. Whether that trade is worth it is a genuine policy dispute, but the bill's scope is comprehensive and its enforcement teeth make the cap effective rather than symbolic.

outcome.mechanism: Durbin introduced it on July 14, 2021, and it was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on July 14, 2021, joined by Senators Merkley, Blumenthal, and Whitehouse as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
That was the bill's last action: it never received a hearing, markup, or vote in committee or on the floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill drew 3 cosponsors, all Democrats, out of a 50-seat Democratic caucus in the Senate, and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, car title, installment, and overdraft-fee lenders keep charging triple-digit rates and billions in annual fees. Borrowers paying those rates are no better off; the only legal 36% cap remains the one covering servicemembers.

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor in the roughly 18 months between referral and the end of the Congress.

against.name: Payday and high-cost consumer lenders
against.role: Industry whose core product the bill would ban
against.what_they_did: The bill's findings describe high-cost lending persisting in all 50 states through state-law loopholes and rate-exportation preemption; opposition from this industry is a recurring feature of national rate-cap proposals, though the record here shows no lobbying events.

sides.party_line_note: All 4 supporters were Democrats — Durbin plus 3 cosponsors from the 48-member Democratic caucus — and no Republican cosponsored; with no recorded votes, the partisan shape comes from sponsorship alone.

industries.note: The bill outlaws their core product: loans averaging about 400% annual interest, a market the bill's findings size at $9 billion a year. The 36% all-in cap makes the business model unworkable.

Overdraft and not-sufficient-funds fees are expressly counted toward the 36% cap, which the findings put at an effective 17,000% annual rate and $14 billion a year in consumer cost. Banks lose that fee revenue and a liquidity product many customers rely on.
Loans averaging about 300% annual interest and $3.8 billion a year in consumer cost, by the bill's findings, would be capped out of existence, and borrowers could void existing charges.

Triple-digit-rate installment loans would be banned, though the bill leaves narrow tolerances — modest application fees, a $20 late fee, a $15 NSF fee — for loans repaid in three or more installments over at least 90 days.

Most credit card APRs sit below 36%, but annual fees, cash advance fees, late fees, and add-on products all count toward the new all-in cap, and statements must show a FAIR all-in rate instead of APR — cutting off some fee revenue and making pricing more transparent to cardholders.
